posts.title: Knee Replacement Rehab: What to Expect During Recovery in Milton
posts.content_raw:
Knee replacement surgery transforms lives, but the surgery is only the beginning. What happens in the weeks and months after surgery determines whether you return to walking, climbing stairs, and living without pain. At Tonic Physio in Milton, Ontario, we guide knee replacement patients through every phase of rehabilitation, from your first steps after surgery to returning to the activities you love.

What You'll Learn: Knee replacement rehabilitation follows a 4-phase timeline spanning 6 to 12 months. Physiotherapy after knee replacement focuses on range of motion, strength, walking, and stair climbing. Each phase has specific exercises, milestones, and precautions.

What Is Knee Replacement Surgery?

Knee replacement surgery, or total knee arthroplasty, replaces the damaged surfaces of your knee joint with artificial components made of metal and plastic. The procedure is recommended for severe osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or post-traumatic arthritis when conservative treatments no longer provide relief. Over 75,000 knee replacements are performed in Canada each year.

Why Physiotherapy Is Critical After Knee Surgery

The new knee joint restores your knee's mechanical structure, but your muscles, tendons, and movement patterns need retraining. Without physiotherapy, patients often develop permanent stiffness, persistent limping, and muscle weakness. A structured physiotherapy program ensures you regain full range of motion, strength, and confidence in your new knee.

How Knee Replacement Differs From Hip Replacement

Knee replacement recovery is typically more painful than hip replacement, especially in the first 2 to 3 weeks. The knee joint requires more aggressive bending to achieve functional range of motion, and scar tissue forms quickly if the knee is not mobilized early. Unlike hip replacement, there are fewer dislocation precautions, but the risk of stiffness is much higher.

Phase 1: Hospital Recovery (Days 1 to 3)

Your rehabilitation begins the day after surgery. Most Ontario patients spend 1 to 3 days in the hospital, where a physiotherapist helps them stand, bend their knee, and take their first steps.

What Happens in Hospital

You will learn to transfer from bed to chair, walk with a walker, and bend your knee to at least 90 degrees. Pain management is critical during this phase because you need to move despite surgical discomfort. Your physiotherapist will teach you ankle pumps, quad sets, and gentle knee bends.

Exercises You Start in Hospital

  • Ankle pumps: Move your foot up and down 20 times every hour to prevent blood clots
  • Quad sets: Tighten your thigh muscle and push your knee into the bed, hold 5 seconds, 10 repetitions
  • Heel slides: Slide your heel toward your buttock, bending your knee as far as comfortable, 10 repetitions
  • Straight leg raises: Tighten your quad and lift your straight leg 6 inches off the bed, hold 3 seconds, 10 repetitions
  • Short arc quads: Place a rolled towel under your knee, lift your foot to straighten your leg, 10 repetitions

Milestone Before Discharge

Before leaving the hospital, you should achieve at least 90 degrees of knee flexion, walk with a walker, transfer independently, and manage stairs with supervision. If you cannot meet these milestones, your doctor may recommend a short rehabilitation facility stay.

Phase 2: Early Home Rehabilitation (Weeks 1 to 4)

Once home in Milton, your focus shifts to regaining knee bending and building walking tolerance. This is the most challenging phase because pain and swelling are still significant.

Week 1 to 2: Range of Motion Focus

Continue your hospital exercises 3 times daily. Add standing exercises: mini squats at a counter, standing knee bends, and assisted heel raises. Walk with your walker every 2 hours for 5 to 10 minutes. Apply ice for 20 minutes after each exercise session to control swelling.

Week 3 to 4: Building Strength

Transition from a walker to a cane if your surgeon approves. Increase knee bending toward 110 degrees. Start stationary bike with no resistance for 5 to 10 minutes. Walk longer distances outdoors on flat surfaces. Your physiotherapy team in Milton will monitor your progress and adjust your exercises weekly.

Pain and Swelling Management

Some pain and swelling are normal for 6 to 8 weeks after surgery. Elevate your leg above heart level when resting, apply ice 3 to 4 times daily, and take prescribed pain medication 30 minutes before exercise. If swelling increases or your knee becomes red and warm, contact your surgeon immediately.

Phase 3: Strengthening and Mobility (Weeks 5 to 12)

This phase focuses on rebuilding the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glute muscles that stabilize your knee. The quadriceps are particularly important because they straighten your knee and prevent buckling when you walk.

Key Exercises for Phase 3

  • Straight leg raises with weight: 2-pound ankle weight, 3 sets of 12
  • Standing hamstring curls: 3 sets of 12 per side
  • Mini squats: Stand at a counter, bend knees 30 to 45 degrees, 3 sets of 12
  • Step-ups: 4-inch platform, leading with the operated leg, 3 sets of 10
  • Stationary bike: 15 to 20 minutes, light resistance
  • Bridging: Lie on your back, lift hips off floor, 3 sets of 12

Walking Progression

By week 6, most patients walk without a cane on flat surfaces. By week 8, you should walk 20 to 30 minutes continuously. If you need guidance, our physiotherapy services in Milton include gait analysis and retraining to ensure you walk without a limp.

Scar Tissue and Knee Stiffness

Surgical scar tissue can limit knee bending if not addressed. Your physiotherapist uses manual therapy to mobilize the scar and patella (kneecap). Gentle stretching targets the hamstrings and calves, which tighten after surgery. If knee stiffness persists despite physiotherapy, your surgeon may discuss manipulation under anesthesia.

Phase 4: Return to Activity (Months 3 to 12)

By month 3, most patients have returned to daily activities. The final phase focuses on returning to recreational activities and maximizing long-term function.

Activities You Can Return To

ActivityTimelineNotes
Walking (unlimited)6 to 8 weeksBest exercise for knee replacement recovery
Swimming6 to 8 weeksOnce incision is fully healed
Stationary bike4 to 6 weeksStart with no resistance
Golf3 to 6 monthsUse a cart initially
Doubles tennis6 monthsAvoid singles (too much pivoting)
Gardening3 monthsUse raised beds, kneelers
Hiking3 to 4 monthsStart with flat trails, progress gradually

Activities to Avoid Long-Term

  • High-impact sports like running, basketball, or soccer
  • Deep squatting past 120 degrees
  • Contact sports
  • Trampolining
  • Singles tennis

How Physiotherapy at Tonic Physio Helps

Our physiotherapy team in Milton has extensive experience with post-surgical rehabilitation. We create individualized programs based on your surgical approach, fitness level, and activity goals.

Your First Appointment

We assess your incision healing, knee range of motion, muscle strength, gait, and stair climbing. We review your surgeon's protocol and design a custom exercise program. Learn more about what to expect at your first appointment.

Ongoing Treatment

Weekly sessions include manual therapy for knee mobilization, progressive exercise instruction, gait retraining, and functional activity practice. We also offer knee pain treatment in Milton for ongoing knee issues after recovery.

Insurance and WSIB Coverage

Most extended health insurance plans in Ontario cover physiotherapy after surgery. If your knee condition resulted from a workplace injury, you may qualify for WSIB coverage in Milton. Contact our team to verify your benefits.

Common Complications and Warning Signs

Most knee replacements heal without major complications, but knowing the warning signs helps you catch problems early.

Blood Clots (DVT)

Deep vein thrombosis is a risk in the first 4 weeks. Symptoms include calf swelling, warmth, and pain. Prevent clots with ankle pumps, walking, and any blood thinners your doctor prescribes.

Infection

Surgical site infections affect roughly 1 to 2 percent of patients. Watch for increasing redness, drainage, fever, or worsening pain after the first week. Early treatment prevents the infection from reaching the joint.

Knee Stiffness (Arthrofibrosis)

Excessive scar tissue can limit knee bending, affecting roughly 5 to 10 percent of patients. The risk is higher if you do not achieve 90 degrees of flexion by week 2. Aggressive early physiotherapy is the best prevention.

Ligament Instability

In rare cases, the ligaments around the new knee become loose, causing instability or giving way. If your knee feels unstable during walking, inform your physiotherapist immediately.

Frequently Asked Questions About Knee Replacement Recovery

How Long Will I Need a Walker or Cane?

Most patients use a walker for 2 to 3 weeks, then transition to a cane for 1 to 2 weeks. By week 4 to 6, many patients walk without any assistive device. Your physiotherapist determines when it is safe to stop based on your gait and balance.

When Can I Drive After Knee Replacement?

For right knee replacements, most surgeons clear driving at 4 to 6 weeks once you can brake safely without pain. For left knee replacements, you may drive as early as 2 to 3 weeks if you are off pain medications.

How Long Does the New Knee Last?

Modern knee replacements last 15 to 25 years in most patients. Longevity depends on your activity level, body weight, and how well you maintain the joint through regular movement and exercise.

Why Does My Knee Click or Pop After Surgery?

Mild clicking or popping is common after knee replacement as the artificial components settle. It is typically painless and not a concern. If clicking is accompanied by pain, swelling, or instability, contact your surgeon or physiotherapist.

How Much Should I Bend My Knee After Surgery?

Aim for 90 degrees of flexion by week 2 and 110 to 115 degrees by week 6. Full functional bending (125 to 135 degrees) typically returns by 3 months. Your physiotherapist will measure your progress and adjust your stretching program.

Can I Kneel After Knee Replacement?

Most surgeons allow kneeling after 3 months if it is comfortable. Kneeling on the operated knee may feel uncomfortable due to the scar and implant. Use a knee pad or cushion for protection.

Recovery Timeline at a Glance

TimeframeMilestoneKey Focus
Days 1 to 390 degree bend, walk with walkerPain control, ankle pumps, heel slides
Weeks 1 to 2Walk independently, home exercisesRange of motion, swelling management
Weeks 3 to 4Cane walking, 110 degree bendStrength, stationary bike
Weeks 5 to 8Walk without cane, stairsQuadriceps strength, gait
Weeks 9 to 12Normal walking, light activityFunctional exercises, balance
Months 3 to 6Golf, swimming, gardeningSport-specific training
Months 6 to 12Full recoveryMaintenance exercise program

Long-Term Care for Your New Knee

Your knee replacement needs ongoing care to last its full lifespan. Regular exercise, weight management, and activity modification keep the joint functioning well for decades.

Maintain an Exercise Routine

Continue a daily exercise routine that includes walking, stationary cycling, and strength training. Strong muscles around the knee absorb shock and reduce wear on the artificial joint. Aim for 30 minutes of exercise 5 days per week.

Manage Your Weight

Every pound of body weight adds 4 pounds of force to your knee during walking. Maintaining a healthy weight reduces stress on the artificial joint and extends its lifespan. If you need guidance, our team can help design a safe exercise program for weight management.

Choose Low-Impact Activities

Walking, swimming, cycling, golf, and hiking are excellent for knee replacement patients. Avoid running, jumping, and contact sports that place high impact loads on the joint. The choices you make about activity directly affect how long your new knee lasts.

Returning to Life in Milton After Knee Replacement

Most knee replacement patients in Milton return to driving by week 4 to 6, return to desk work at 6 to 8 weeks, and resume most recreational activities by 3 months. Your individual timeline depends on your surgical approach, fitness before surgery, and commitment to physiotherapy.

Call us at (905) 878-7775 to book your post-surgical physiotherapy assessment, or book online through JaneApp for an appointment that fits your schedule. Our team in Milton will guide you from your first steps after surgery to a full return to the activities you love.

posts.title: How to Fix Bad Posture: A Complete Guide for Milton Residents
posts.content_raw:
Bad posture is something most Milton residents brush off as a minor habit. A slouched shoulder here, a forward head there. Over weeks and months, though, those small habits compound into real pain, stiffness, and lost mobility that can disrupt work, sleep, and daily life.

The good news is that posture is not a fixed trait. With the right combination of awareness, targeted exercises, and professional guidance, most posture problems respond well to treatment. At Tonic Physio in Milton, our team helps people of every age and activity level understand the root causes of their posture issues and build lasting correction plans.

This guide breaks down what bad posture actually is, the most common types, the symptoms it creates, and how to fix bad posture with a structured approach that works in real life.

What You'll Learn

- What bad posture is and why it develops - The five most common types of posture dysfunction - How poor posture affects your neck, back, head, and breathing - Seven practical exercises to correct posture at home - How physiotherapy in Milton builds a lasting correction plan - Realistic timelines for posture improvement

What Is Bad Posture?

Bad posture is any sustained body position that places disproportionate stress on muscles, joints, and ligaments outside their natural alignment, leading to fatigue, strain, and over time, pain or injury.

Your body is designed to move through balanced positions. When you hold a slouched, tilted, or forward-shifted position for hours at a stretch, certain muscles overwork while others weaken from underuse. Over time, the body adapts to that new position as its baseline, making good posture feel unnatural and hard to hold.

Posture problems are rarely about laziness. They develop from repeated daily patterns. The pattern could be hunching over a laptop, cradling a phone between ear and shoulder, or standing with weight on one leg. The body simply learns what you do most often.

5 Types of Bad Posture

Posture problems tend to follow recognizable patterns. Identifying which pattern you fall into is the first step toward targeted correction. The five most common types are forward head posture, rounded shoulders, anterior pelvic tilt, flat back, and scoliosis.

Forward Head Posture

Forward head posture, sometimes called "text neck," occurs when the head juts forward of the shoulders instead of stacking directly over the spine. For every inch the head drifts forward, the neck muscles bear an extra 10 to 12 pounds of load.

This pattern is extremely common among people who work at screens, commute long distances, or spend hours on a phone. Over time it contributes to chronic neck stiffness, tension headaches, and upper back pain. We explore this pattern in depth in our article on physiotherapy for forward head posture.

Rounded Shoulders

Rounded shoulders develop when the chest muscles tighten and the upper back muscles weaken, pulling the shoulders forward into a hunched position. The shoulder blades drift apart instead of sitting flat against the rib cage.

This posture is common in desk workers, drivers, and anyone who spends long periods reaching forward. Left uncorrected, rounded shoulders can restrict shoulder mobility, contribute to rotator cuff strain, and worsen forward head posture.

Anterior Pelvic Tilt

Anterior pelvic tilt, sometimes called "lower crossed posture," happens when the pelvis tips forward, creating an exaggerated arch in the lower back. The stomach protrudes and the buttocks stick out, even in lean individuals.

This pattern stems from tight hip flexors, weak abdominal muscles, and weak glutes. It is common in people who sit for most of the day. Anterior pelvic tilt frequently drives lower back pain and hip tightness, both of which respond well to targeted physiotherapy.

Flat Back

Flat back posture is the opposite problem. The natural curve of the lower spine flattens out, so the pelvis tucks under and the upper back often compensates by rounding forward. The whole trunk leans slightly backward to stay balanced.

Flat back can develop after long periods of sitting in a tucked position, after certain spinal surgeries, or from muscle imbalances around the hips and spine. It often causes stiffness, hamstring tightness, and difficulty standing for long stretches.

Scoliosis

Scoliosis is a sideways curvature of the spine, often developing in adolescence but sometimes appearing in adulthood from degenerative changes. The curve can create uneven shoulders, a prominent shoulder blade, or an uneven waistline.

Mild scoliosis often goes unnoticed until a routine screening or posture assessment flags it. Moderate to severe curves require professional management, which may include targeted exercise, bracing, or in some cases referral to a specialist.

What Causes Bad Posture

Posture problems rarely come from a single source. They build from daily patterns repeated thousands of times. Understanding your personal pattern is what makes correction effective.

Desk Work and Sitting

Long hours at a desk are one of the biggest posture drivers in Milton. Sitting collapses the hips into a tight, shortened position, weakens the glutes, rounds the upper back, and pushes the head forward. A poorly set up workspace accelerates all of this. A proper workplace ergonomics assessment in Milton addresses desk height, screen position, chair support, and daily movement habits.

Phone and Screen Use

The average Canadian spends several hours daily on a phone or tablet. Each session tilts the head down and forward, loading the neck muscles far beyond their design capacity. Repeated daily, this drives the forward head pattern. Holding the phone at eye level and taking movement breaks helps, but once the pattern sets in, targeted exercise is usually needed to reverse it.

Muscle Imbalance

Posture is a balance between muscle groups working in pairs. When one side tightens and the other weakens, alignment drifts. Tight chest muscles pull shoulders forward. Weak deep neck flexors let the head drift. Tight hip flexors tilt the pelvis forward. Strengthening the weak side and stretching the tight side is what corrective exercise is built on.

Stress and Tension

Stress increases muscle tension, especially in the neck, shoulders, and jaw. People under chronic stress often unconsciously hunch and guard their upper body, reinforcing rounded shoulders and forward head patterns. Movement, breathing work, and manual therapy all help reset this tension. Deep tissue massage in Milton and manual osteopathy in Milton both complement physiotherapy for this layer.

How Bad Posture Affects Your Body

Posture is not a cosmetic issue. Sustained misalignment creates real physical symptoms that gradually limit what you can do. Four of the most common are neck pain, back pain, headaches, and breathing changes.

Neck Pain

Forward head posture overloads the small muscles of the neck and the joints of the cervical spine. The result is stiffness, aching, and reduced range of motion that worsens through the day. Our guide to effective neck pain treatments covers how physiotherapy addresses this layer.

Back Pain

Anterior pelvic tilt, flat back, and rounded shoulders all shift loads onto the spine in ways it is not built to handle. Lower back pain is one of the most common consequences, especially in people who sit for long stretches. Our articles on physiotherapy for lower back pain and the best physiotherapy exercises for lower back pain walk through how we approach it.

Headaches

Tension headaches often trace back to the neck. Tight suboccipital muscles at the base of the skull, overloaded by forward head posture, refer pain into the temples, forehead, and behind the eyes. Correcting the postural driver is usually more effective than relying on pain medication alone.

Breathing and Energy

A slouched, compressed posture reduces the room your diaphragm has to move. Shallow breathing follows, which lowers oxygen delivery and contributes to fatigue. Many people are surprised how much energy returns once their posture opens up and their rib cage can move freely again.

7 Exercises to Fix Bad Posture

The right exercises depend on your specific posture pattern, but the seven below cover the most common weak links. Do them daily, move slowly, and stop if any cause sharp pain. None of these replace a proper assessment.

Chin Tucks

Sit or stand tall. Gently draw your chin straight back as if making a double chin, keeping your eyes level. Hold for five seconds and release. Aim for two sets of ten. This strengthens the deep neck flexors and directly counters forward head posture.

Wall Angels

Stand with your back against a wall, heels a few inches out, head and shoulders touching. Raise your arms into a goalpost position against the wall, then slide them up and down slowly, keeping contact. Two sets of eight builds upper back strength and opens the chest.

Doorway Chest Stretch

Stand in a doorway with one forearm on the frame, elbow bent at 90 degrees and slightly above shoulder height. Step gently forward until you feel a stretch across the chest. Hold 30 seconds per side. This releases the tight chest muscles that pull shoulders forward.

Shoulder Blade Squeezes

Sit or stand tall and squeeze your shoulder blades together and down, as if trying to hold a pencil between them. Hold five seconds and release. Two sets of ten strengthens the rhomboids and lower trapezius, the muscles that hold the shoulders back.

Glute Bridges

Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat. Squeeze your glutes and lift your hips until your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Lower slowly. Two sets of twelve strengthens the glutes and counters anterior pelvic tilt.

Cat-Cow Stretch

On hands and knees, alternate slowly between arching your back up toward the ceiling and letting it sag toward the floor, moving with your breath. Eight to ten slow cycles mobilizes the whole spine and counters the stiffness of prolonged sitting.

Plank Hold

Start on forearms and toes, body in a straight line from head to heels, core braced. Hold 20 to 30 seconds and repeat three times. The plank builds the deep core stability that supports a neutral spine in every other posture.

How Physiotherapy Fixes Posture in Milton

Home exercises help, but lasting posture correction usually needs a structured plan. Physiotherapy in Milton at Tonic Physio combines assessment, hands-on treatment, and a personalized exercise program to address the root causes, not just the symptoms.

Posture Assessment

Your physiotherapist begins with a full assessment that looks at standing posture, spinal curves, shoulder position, pelvic tilt, and movement patterns. They identify which muscles are tight, which are weak, and which habits are driving the dysfunction. This assessment is what makes the rest of the plan targeted rather than generic.

Manual Therapy

Tight joints and restricted muscles often need hands-on treatment before exercise can do its job. Manual therapy techniques, including joint mobilization, soft tissue release, and myofascial work, restore range of motion and reduce pain so you can actually perform your corrective exercises well. For spine and pelvic restrictions, manual osteopathy in Milton is another effective option we offer alongside physiotherapy.

Personalized Exercise Program

Your physiotherapist builds a custom exercise program targeting your specific posture pattern. The program progresses over time as your strength and mobility improve, so the changes stick rather than fading between sessions. For combined neck and back patterns, our back and neck pain program in Milton addresses both areas together.

Posture Correction vs Quick Fixes

The market is full of posture braces, apps, and gadgets promising instant results. Understanding the difference between genuine correction and quick fixes helps you spend your time and money well.

ApproachCorrection (Physiotherapy)Quick Fixes (Braces, Gadgets)
TargetRoot muscle and joint causesExternal support only
TimeframeWeeks to monthsImmediate but temporary
Lasting resultYes, changes holdNo, reverts when removed
Effort requiredActive exercises and habit changePassive, minimal effort
Cost over timeOne targeted programRepeated purchases, devices
Side effectsStronger, more mobile bodyWeaker muscles from reliance

The pattern to watch for is passive devices that feel helpful but let your muscles do less work. Real correction makes your body stronger and more aware, so it holds good posture on its own.

How Long Does Posture Correction Take

Posture correction is a gradual process. Timelines depend on how long the pattern has been in place, how consistently you follow your program, and whether underlying joint or tissue restrictions are involved.

StageTimeframeWhat You Feel
Awareness and mobilityWeeks 1 to 2Less stiffness, easier neutral posture
Early strength gainsWeeks 3 to 6Posture holds longer, less end-of-day pain
Lasting strengthWeeks 7 to 12Good posture feels natural, symptoms fade
MaintenanceOngoingPeriodic exercise keeps gains for life

Most people notice meaningful improvement within four to eight weeks of consistent work. Longer-standing patterns, especially those involving joint stiffness, often need three months or more. Your physiotherapist sets realistic milestones based on your specific assessment.

Better Posture for Life in Milton

Fixing bad posture is one of the highest-leverage changes you can make for your long-term health. Less pain, more energy, better movement, and a body that feels easier to live in are all realistic outcomes when you commit to a structured plan.

At Tonic Physio in Milton, we start every posture case with a thorough assessment so your program targets your actual pattern rather than a generic checklist. If you are dealing with neck pain, back pain, headaches, or stiffness that you suspect is posture related, we would like to help you build a plan that lasts.

Not sure what to expect? Our guide on what to expect at your first physiotherapy appointment walks you through the process from check-in to treatment plan.

Ready to fix bad posture for good? Call Tonic Physio at (905) 875-2225 or book your assessment online through JaneApp. Our Milton clinic team will help you understand what is driving your posture issues and build a plan that fits your life.

posts.title: 7 TMJ Exercises You Can Do at Home for Jaw Pain Relief in Milton
posts.content_raw:
Jaw pain affects millions of Canadians, and many do not realize that physiotherapy can help. The temporomandibular joint, or TMJ, connects your jaw to your skull and is one of the most complex joints in your body. When it stops working properly, simple actions like eating, talking, and yawning become painful. At Tonic Physio in Milton, Ontario, we treat TMJ dysfunction regularly and teach patients exercises they can do at home to speed up their recovery.
What You'll Learn: TMJ exercises can reduce jaw pain, improve mobility, and prevent clicking or locking. This guide covers 7 effective exercises, home pain relief tips, and when to see a physiotherapist for TMJ treatment in Milton.

What Is TMJ and Why Does It Hurt?

The temporomandibular joint (TMJ) is the hinge joint that connects your lower jaw (mandible) to your skull (temporal bone) on each side of your face. It allows you to open and close your mouth, move your jaw side to side, and chew food. TMJ dysfunction, also called TMD, occurs when the joint, the muscles around it, or the disc inside the joint become inflamed or misaligned.

How Common Is TMJ Pain?

Roughly 5 to 12 percent of adults experience TMJ pain at some point. Women are affected twice as often as men, particularly between ages 20 and 50. In Milton and the Halton Region, we see TMJ patients from all backgrounds: office workers who clench their jaws at their desks, athletes who grind their teeth during competition, and parents who carry tension in their jaw from daily stress.

Why TMJ Pain Often Goes Untreated

Many people assume jaw pain will go away on its own or think it is a dental problem. While dentists can address teeth grinding with night guards, the joint and muscle dysfunction often requires physiotherapy. Our TMJ treatment in Milton addresses the root cause through manual therapy, exercise, and posture correction.

Symptoms of TMJ Dysfunction

TMJ dysfunction produces a range of symptoms that extend beyond the jaw itself. Recognizing these symptoms early helps you start treatment before the condition worsens.

Jaw Pain and Tenderness

Pain in the jaw joint is the most common symptom. It may be sharp when you open wide or dull and constant when resting. Tenderness usually appears just in front of the ear, where the TMJ sits.

Clicking, Popping, or Grinding

Many TMJ patients hear clicking or popping sounds when they open their mouth or chew. These sounds occur when the articular disc inside the joint shifts out of position. While not always painful, they signal that the joint mechanics need attention.

Headaches and Facial Pain

TMJ dysfunction is a major cause of tension headaches. The muscles that control your jaw connect to your temples and the base of your skull. When these muscles stay tight, the tension radiates upward and creates headache pain. If you experience frequent headaches, our headache and migraine treatment in Milton can identify whether TMJ is the source.

Limited Jaw Opening

A healthy jaw opens 40 to 55 millimeters, which is about three fingers wide. If your opening is less than 35 millimeters or feels restricted, the joint may be inflamed or the disc may be blocking the path.

What Causes TMJ Pain

Understanding your TMJ cause helps determine which exercises and treatments will work best for you. The most common causes fall into four categories.

Teeth Grinding and Clenching (Bruxism)

Grinding or clenching your teeth, especially during sleep, places constant pressure on the TMJ and surrounding muscles. Many people are unaware they grind until a partner mentions it or they wake up with jaw pain. A night guard from your dentist protects your teeth, but physiotherapy addresses the muscle tension and joint dysfunction that grinding creates.

Stress and Muscle Tension

Stress causes you to unconsciously tighten your jaw muscles throughout the day. Over time, this chronic tension fatigues the muscles and misaligns the joint. Stress management techniques, combined with jaw exercises, break this tension cycle.

Poor Posture

Forward head posture directly affects TMJ alignment. When your head sits forward, your lower jaw shifts back, compressing the TMJ. Correcting neck posture is often a key part of TMJ treatment. Learn more about forward head posture correction on our blog.

Arthritis and Joint Degeneration

Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis can affect the TMJ, causing cartilage breakdown, inflammation, and pain. If you have arthritis in other joints and are experiencing jaw pain, the TMJ may be involved. Our team can also help with cervical spondylosis treatment if neck degeneration is contributing.

7 TMJ Exercises to Do at Home

These exercises target the muscles and joints that control jaw movement. Do them twice daily, gently and consistently. Stop any exercise that increases your pain.

1. Relaxed Jaw Exercise

Place your tongue gently on the roof of your mouth, just behind your upper front teeth. Allow your teeth to separate and your jaw to relax. Hold this position for 30 seconds. This exercise trains your jaw to rest in a neutral position, reducing unconscious clenching.

2. Chin Tucks

Sit or stand tall. Pull your head straight back as if making a double chin, keeping your eyes level. Hold for 5 seconds, then relax. Repeat 10 times. Chin tucks correct the forward head posture that contributes to TMJ dysfunction and relieve tension in the muscles connecting your neck and jaw.

3. Goldfish Exercise (Partial Opening)

Place one finger on your TMJ (just in front of your ear) and another finger on your chin. Drop your tongue to the roof of your mouth. Slowly open your jaw halfway, then close. Repeat 10 times. This exercise gently mobilizes the joint while teaching proper opening mechanics.

4. Goldfish Exercise (Full Opening)

Use the same finger positions as the partial exercise. This time, open your jaw as wide as comfortable without pain. Close slowly. Repeat 10 times. This exercise restores full range of motion in the joint.

5. Tongue to Roof Breathing

Place your tongue on the roof of your mouth. Breathe in through your nose for 4 counts, then out for 4 counts. Continue for 2 minutes. This exercise relaxes your jaw muscles, promotes nasal breathing, and reduces the mouth breathing that stresses the TMJ.

6. Side-to-Side Jaw Movement

Place a clean pencil or stick between your front teeth. Slowly move your jaw to the left, hold 2 seconds, then move to the right, hold 2 seconds. Repeat 10 times per side. This exercise improves lateral TMJ mobility, which is often restricted in dysfunction.

7. Forward Jaw Movement

With the pencil between your front teeth, slowly move your lower jaw forward so your bottom teeth extend past your top teeth. Hold 2 seconds, then return. Repeat 10 times. This exercise mobilizes the TMJ in the forward plane, completing the full range of motion.

Tips for TMJ Pain Relief at Home

Exercise alone is not enough. These daily habits complement your TMJ exercises and speed up recovery.

Apply Heat or Ice

Apply a warm, moist towel to your jaw for 15 minutes before exercising to relax muscles. After exercising, apply an ice pack wrapped in a cloth for 10 minutes to reduce inflammation. Alternate heat and ice if your pain is acute.

Eat Soft Foods

Avoid hard, chewy, or crunchy foods for the first 2 weeks of treatment. Choose soups, smoothies, scrambled eggs, pasta, and soft vegetables. Cut food into small pieces to reduce the width of your jaw opening during meals.

Sleep on Your Back

Sleeping on your side or stomach puts pressure on your jaw. Sleep on your back with a supportive pillow that keeps your neck aligned. If you must sleep on your side, use a pillow between your shoulder and jaw to avoid compression.

Manage Stress

Stress is a major TMJ trigger. Practice deep breathing, meditation, or progressive muscle relaxation for 10 minutes daily. If you notice yourself clenching during the day, pause and do the relaxed jaw exercise.

When to See a Physiotherapist for TMJ Pain

Home exercises help mild TMJ pain, but certain symptoms require professional treatment. Do not wait if you experience any of the following.
  • Jaw pain that lasts more than 2 weeks despite home exercises
  • Jaw locking open or closed
  • Inability to open your mouth more than two fingers wide
  • Pain that radiates from your jaw to your temple, ear, or neck
  • Frequent headaches originating from your jaw or temple area
  • Difficulty chewing or biting due to jaw misalignment

How Physiotherapy Treats TMJ in Milton

At Tonic Physio, our physiotherapy services in Milton include specialized TMJ treatment that goes beyond home exercises. We combine hands-on therapy, targeted exercises, and posture correction to address the root cause of your jaw pain.

Manual Therapy for TMJ

Your physiotherapist uses gentle hands-on techniques to mobilize the TMJ, release tight jaw muscles, and improve joint alignment. Manual therapy provides immediate relief that exercises alone cannot achieve. Our manual osteopathy in Milton complements TMJ treatment by addressing whole-body alignment issues that contribute to jaw dysfunction.

Exercise Prescription

We design a custom exercise program based on your specific TMJ dysfunction pattern. If your disc is displaced, we prescribe specific mobilization exercises. If muscle tension is the main issue, we focus on relaxation and stretching. If posture is the driver, we include neck and upper back exercises. Learn more about what to expect at your first appointment.

Massage Therapy for TMJ

Massage therapy releases the tight muscles around your jaw, face, and neck. Our indie head massage in Milton specifically targets the head, face, and neck muscles that contribute to TMJ pain. Regular massage sessions prevent tension from rebuilding between physiotherapy visits.

TMJ Exercises vs Other Treatment Options

Treatment What It Does Best For
Home exercises Mobilizes joint, relaxes muscles Mild pain, prevention
Physiotherapy Manual therapy + exercise + posture Moderate to severe TMJ dysfunction
Massage therapy Releases tight jaw and neck muscles Muscle tension, stress-related TMJ
Dental night guard Prevents teeth grinding at night Bruxism, tooth damage prevention
Medication Temporary pain and inflammation relief Acute flare-ups, short-term use

How Long Does TMJ Treatment Take

TMJ recovery timelines vary based on the severity of dysfunction and how long you have had symptoms. Most patients see noticeable improvement within 4 to 8 weeks of consistent exercise and physiotherapy.

Acute TMJ Pain (Less Than 6 Weeks)

If your jaw pain started recently, you can expect faster recovery. Acute TMJ pain often responds to home exercises, ice, and soft food within 2 to 4 weeks. One or two physiotherapy sessions can accelerate recovery by identifying the specific joint or muscle issue.

Chronic TMJ Pain (More Than 3 Months)

Chronic TMJ dysfunction takes longer to treat because the muscle patterns and joint alignment have become habitual. Expect 6 to 12 weeks of regular physiotherapy, home exercises, and possibly massage therapy. Chronic cases often involve neck posture issues that need simultaneous treatment.
Severity Timeline Sessions Needed
Mild (occasional pain) 2 to 4 weeks 1 to 2 sessions
Moderate (daily pain) 4 to 8 weeks 4 to 6 sessions
Chronic (long-standing) 8 to 12 weeks 6 to 10 sessions
Severe (locking, severe pain) 3 to 6 months 10+ sessions

Preventing TMJ Pain From Coming Back

Once your TMJ pain resolves, prevention keeps it from returning. The habits that caused the dysfunction in the first place need to change permanently.

Maintain Proper Jaw Posture

Keep your teeth slightly apart and your tongue on the roof of your mouth when resting. This neutral jaw position prevents unconscious clenching and keeps the TMJ aligned throughout the day.

Continue Your Exercises

Even after pain resolves, continue the relaxed jaw exercise and chin tucks once daily. These exercises maintain joint mobility and muscle balance, preventing the stiffness that leads to recurrence.

Address Stress Proactively

Stress is the most common TMJ trigger. Build a daily stress management routine that includes deep breathing, exercise, or mindfulness. When stress increases, increase your TMJ exercises from once to twice daily.

Get Regular Massage Therapy

Monthly massage therapy sessions prevent tension from building up in your jaw, face, and neck muscles. Regular head and neck massage in Milton is an effective preventive measure for chronic TMJ patients.

Relieving TMJ Pain in Milton

TMJ pain does not have to be permanent. With consistent home exercises, proper habits, and professional physiotherapy, most TMJ patients see significant improvement within 4 to 8 weeks. Call us at (905) 878-7775 to book a TMJ assessment, or book online through JaneApp for an appointment that fits your schedule. Our team will evaluate your jaw, design a custom treatment plan, and teach you the exercises that will keep your TMJ pain-free for the long term.

posts.title: Workplace Ergonomics: How to Prevent Pain at Your Desk in Milton
posts.content_raw:
If you work at a desk in Milton, you probably spend more time sitting than sleeping. The average office worker sits for nearly 10 hours each day, and most of those hours involve a screen, a keyboard, and a chair that may not fit your body. Poor workplace ergonomics is one of the leading causes of neck pain, back pain, and repetitive strain injuries we treat at Tonic Physio in Milton, Ontario.
What You'll Learn: Proper workplace ergonomics can prevent up to 60% of desk-related musculoskeletal injuries. This guide covers desk setup, chair positioning, monitor height, keyboard placement, daily stretches, and when to see a physiotherapist in Milton for work-related pain.

What Is Workplace Ergonomics?

Workplace ergonomics is the science of designing your work environment to fit your body, not the other way around. When your desk, chair, monitor, keyboard, and mouse are positioned correctly, your muscles stay relaxed, your joints stay aligned, and your risk of pain drops significantly.

The Core Principles of Ergonomic Design

Good ergonomics follows three rules: neutral posture, minimal force, and frequent movement. Neutral posture means your spine is stacked, shoulders are relaxed, and wrists are straight. Minimal force means you are not gripping, reaching, or pressing harder than necessary. Frequent movement means you change positions every 30 to 60 minutes, even if your setup is perfect.

Why Ergonomics Matters for Milton Workers

Milton is one of the fastest-growing communities in the Halton Region, with thousands of residents commuting to office jobs in Toronto, Mississauga, and Brampton. Many of these workers come home with stiff necks, aching lower backs, and tingling hands. The commute itself adds to the problem: driving posture is often as bad as desk posture, and combining both creates a full day of strain.

How Poor Desk Setup Causes Pain

Your body is not designed for 8 hours of sitting. When your workspace forces your body out of neutral alignment, specific muscle groups compensate, fatigue, and eventually fail. Understanding which setups cause which problems helps you target your fixes.

Forward Head Posture and Neck Pain

When your monitor sits too low, your head tilts forward. For every inch your head moves forward, your neck muscles carry an additional 10 pounds of load. After a full workday, that is like holding a bowling ball with your neck. Over weeks and months, this leads to chronic neck pain, headaches, and even forward head posture dysfunction that requires physiotherapy to correct.

Lower Back Pain from Poor Chair Support

When your chair lacks lumbar support, your lower back rounds into a C-shape. This posture puts pressure on your spinal discs and overstretches your back ligaments. Sitting in this position for hours is a direct path to herniated discs and chronic lower back pain. If you already experience back pain, our physiotherapy services in Milton can help you recover and learn proper sitting mechanics.

Wrist and Shoulder Strain from Keyboard Height

If your desk is too high, your shoulders shrug. If your keyboard is too far, you reach forward and your wrists bend upward. Both positions strain the rotator cuff muscles and compress the carpal tunnel. Over time, this leads to shoulder impingement, wrist tendonitis, and numbness in your hands.

The 6-Step Desk Setup Checklist for Milton Workers

Use this checklist to adjust your workspace in under 15 minutes. Each step targets a specific pain zone and follows the neutral posture principle.

Step 1: Chair Height

Set your chair so your feet rest flat on the floor with your knees at 90 degrees. If your feet do not reach the floor, use a footrest. Your hips should be slightly above your knees, not level. This angle keeps your lower back in a natural curve.

Step 2: Lumbar Support

Position the backrest so the curve sits in the small of your back, around belt level. If your chair has no adjustable lumbar support, place a small rolled towel between your back and the chair. This support prevents the C-shape slump that causes disc pressure.

Step 3: Monitor Distance and Height

Place your monitor an arm's length away. The top of the screen should sit at or slightly below eye level so your gaze tilts 10 to 20 degrees downward. If you use a laptop, raise it on a stand and use a separate keyboard and mouse. Looking down at a laptop screen for 8 hours is the number one cause of neck pain we see in Milton office workers.

Step 4: Keyboard and Mouse Position

Keep your keyboard close enough that your elbows stay at your sides at 90 to 100 degrees. Your wrists should be straight, not bent up or down. Position your mouse next to your keyboard at the same height. If your wrists still bend, try a keyboard with a negative tilt.

Step 5: Lighting and Screen Glare

Position your screen perpendicular to windows to reduce glare. Poor lighting causes you to lean forward and squint, which strains your neck and eyes. Use a desk lamp for document reading instead of relying on screen brightness alone.

Step 6: Movement Schedule

Set a timer for every 30 minutes. Stand up, stretch, or walk for at least 60 seconds. Movement restores blood flow, resets your posture, and prevents muscle fatigue from accumulating. Even the best ergonomic setup fails if you sit still for 3 hours straight.

5 Stretches Every Desk Worker Should Do Daily

These stretches target the muscle groups most affected by desk work. Do them at your desk, in your office, or during your commute break. Each stretch takes under 60 seconds.

1. Neck Retraction

Sit tall and pull your head straight back as if making a double chin. Hold for 5 seconds, repeat 10 times. This stretch reverses forward head posture and strengthens the deep neck flexors that keep your head aligned.

2. Shoulder Blade Squeeze

Sit upright and squeeze your shoulder blades together as if holding a pencil between them. Hold for 5 seconds, repeat 10 times. This stretch opens your chest, activates your rhomboids, and counters the rounded shoulder posture from keyboard work.

3. Standing Forward Fold

Stand up, bend your knees slightly, and fold forward from the hips. Let your arms hang and hold for 20 seconds. This stretch decompresses your lower back and stretches your hamstrings, which tighten from prolonged sitting.

4. Wrist Flexor Stretch

Extend your arm with the palm facing up. Use your other hand to gently pull your fingers back toward your forearm. Hold 15 seconds per side. This stretch relieves carpal tunnel pressure and forearm tension from typing.

5. Thoracic Rotation

Sit tall, cross your arms over your chest, and rotate your torso to one side. Hold 5 seconds, then rotate to the other side. Repeat 10 times. This stretch mobilizes your mid-spine, which stiffens from sitting and contributes to neck and shoulder pain.

Common Ergonomic Mistakes That Cause Pain

Most desk workers make the same four mistakes. Each one forces your body out of neutral alignment and creates a specific pattern of pain.
Mistake What Happens Pain Result
Laptop on desk without stand Screen too low, neck bent forward Neck pain, headaches, upper back tension
Chair too low, no footrest Hips below knees, lower back rounds Lower back pain, hip tightness
Monitor too far away Leaning forward, shoulders raised Shoulder pain, eye strain, neck fatigue
Phone tucked to ear Neck tilted sideways for calls One-sided neck pain, trapezius strain

The Laptop Trap

Laptops are designed for portability, not ergonomics. The screen and keyboard are too close together, forcing you to choose between neck strain or shoulder strain. If you work on a laptop full-time, invest in a laptop stand, an external keyboard, and a mouse. This setup costs under $100 and prevents thousands in physiotherapy bills.

The "I'll Fix It Later" Mindset

The most common mistake is ignoring early pain signals. A stiff neck at 3pm is not normal. Tingling in your fingers is not normal. These signals mean your body is compensating for a bad setup. The longer you wait, the harder the pattern is to reverse. Our workplace ergonomics assessment in Milton can identify and fix these issues before they become chronic.

How Physiotherapy Helps Desk Workers in Milton

Even with a perfect desk setup, years of poor posture leave damage in your muscles, joints, and movement patterns. Physiotherapy addresses this damage directly. At Tonic Physio in Milton, we treat desk workers every day and know exactly which patterns to target.

What a Physiotherapy Assessment Covers

Your first visit includes a full postural assessment, range of motion testing, and muscle screening. We check your neck, shoulders, mid-back, lower back, and wrists. We identify which muscles are tight, which are weak, and which movement patterns need retraining. Learn more about what to expect at your first physiotherapy appointment before you book.

Manual Therapy for Desk-Related Tension

Hands-on treatment releases tight neck muscles, mobilizes stiff thoracic joints, and decompresses the lower back. Manual therapy provides immediate relief and restores movement that stretching alone cannot achieve. Our manual osteopathy in Milton complements physiotherapy by addressing whole-body alignment.

Exercise Prescription for Long-Term Relief

We design a custom exercise program targeting your specific weak points. If your deep neck flexors are weak, we prescribe chin tucks. If your glutes are inactive from sitting, we prescribe bridge exercises. If your thoracic spine is stiff, we prescribe rotation drills. These exercises retrain your body to hold neutral posture naturally, even after a full day at your desk.

Massage Therapy for Muscle Recovery

Deep tissue massage releases chronic tension in the neck, shoulders, and lower back. Regular massage therapy sessions prevent minor tightness from becoming major pain. Our deep tissue massage therapy in Milton targets the exact muscle groups that suffer most from desk work.

When to See a Physiotherapist for Desk Pain

Not every ache requires a clinic visit, but certain symptoms signal that your body needs professional help. If you experience any of the following, book a physiotherapy assessment in Milton.

Red Flag Symptoms

  • Pain that lasts more than 2 weeks despite stretching and posture corrections
  • Numbness or tingling in your hands, fingers, or arms
  • Headaches that start at the base of your skull and move forward
  • Pain that radiates from your neck into your shoulder or arm
  • Stiffness in your neck or back that is worse in the morning
  • Pain that interferes with sleep or daily activities

WSIB Coverage for Workplace Injuries

If your desk-related pain developed as a direct result of your job, you may qualify for WSIB coverage. Ontario's Workplace Safety and Insurance Board covers physiotherapy for repetitive strain injuries, including carpal tunnel syndrome, tendonitis, and chronic back pain from poor workplace ergonomics. Learn more about our WSIB care programs in Milton and how we handle your claim from start to finish.

Quick Reference: Ergonomic Setup by Body Part

Body Part Target Position Common Mistake
Eyes Top of screen at eye level Screen too low, looking down
Shoulders Relaxed, not raised Desk too high, shrugging
Elbows 90 to 100 degrees, at your sides Reaching forward for keyboard
Wrists Straight, not bent Keyboard too high, wrists extended
Hips Slightly above knees, 95 to 105 degrees Chair too low, hips below knees
Feet Flat on floor or footrest Dangling feet, knee pressure

Building Better Work Habits in Milton

Fixing your desk is the first step. Building better daily habits keeps the pain from coming back. Small changes in your routine add up to major reductions in pain over weeks and months.

Move More, Sit Less

The human body thrives on movement. Aim for 2 minutes of movement every 30 minutes. Walk to the water cooler, do a lap around the office, or stretch at your desk. If you commute to Toronto or Mississauga, use rest stops on the QEW to walk and reset your posture.

Invest in Your Chair

You spend more time in your office chair than your bed. A quality ergonomic chair with adjustable lumbar support, armrests, and seat depth is the single best investment for preventing desk pain. If your employer does not provide one, ask. Ontario employers have a duty to provide safe workstations under the Occupational Health and Safety Act.

Listen to Your Body

Pain is information, not a nuisance. When your neck hurts at 2pm, it means something in your setup or routine needs to change. Do not wait until the pain becomes constant. The earlier you address the cause, the faster and easier the fix.

Take the Next Step Toward a Pain-Free Workday

Proper workplace ergonomics can prevent most desk-related injuries, but existing pain needs professional treatment. If you live or work in Milton, Burlington, Oakville, or anywhere in the Halton Region, Tonic Physio is here to help you work without pain. Call us at (905) 878-7775 to book a physiotherapy assessment, or book online through JaneApp for an appointment that fits your schedule. Our team in Milton will assess your posture, treat your pain, and design a plan that keeps you comfortable at your desk for the long term.

posts.title: Hip Replacement Recovery: A Week-by-Week Physiotherapy Timeline
posts.content_raw:
Hip replacement surgery is one of the most successful orthopedic procedures in Canada, with over 70,000 hip replacements performed each year. But the surgery itself is only half the recovery. What you do in the weeks and months after surgery determines whether you return to walking, golfing, or playing with your grandchildren without pain. At Tonic Physio in Milton, Ontario, we guide hip replacement patients through every phase of rehabilitation.
What You'll Learn: Hip replacement recovery takes 6 to 12 weeks for basic function and up to 12 months for full strength. Physiotherapy after hip replacement follows a 4-phase timeline: hospital recovery, early home rehab, strengthening, and return to activity. Each phase has specific exercises, precautions, and milestones.

What Is Hip Replacement Surgery?

Hip replacement surgery, or total hip arthroplasty, replaces the damaged ball and socket of your hip joint with artificial components made of metal, ceramic, or plastic. The procedure is typically recommended for severe osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or hip fractures that no longer respond to conservative treatment.

Why Physiotherapy Is Essential After Hip Surgery

The new hip joint restores your hip's mechanical structure, but your muscles, tendons, and nervous system need retraining to use it properly. Without physiotherapy, patients often develop compensatory movement patterns, persistent limping, and muscle weakness that limit long-term outcomes. A structured physiotherapy program ensures you regain range of motion, strength, and confidence in your new hip.

The Anterior vs Posterior Approach

Your surgeon's approach affects your recovery timeline. Anterior hip replacement accesses the joint from the front, sparing key muscles, and typically allows faster walking and fewer precautions. Posterior hip replacement accesses the joint from the back and requires stricter bending precautions for 6 to 8 weeks. Your physiotherapist at Tonic Physio will tailor your program to your specific surgical approach.

Phase 1: Hospital Recovery (Days 1 to 3)

Your rehabilitation begins the day after surgery. Most patients in Ontario spend 1 to 3 days in the hospital, where a physiotherapist helps them stand, take their first steps, and learn safe movement techniques.

What Happens in Hospital

You will learn to sit up, transfer from bed to chair, and walk with a walker or crutches. Your physiotherapist will teach you hip precautions to prevent dislocation, especially if you had a posterior approach. These precautions include not bending your hip past 90 degrees, not crossing your legs, and not rotating your foot inward.

Exercises You Start in Hospital

  • Ankle pumps: Move your foot up and down 20 times every hour to prevent blood clots
  • Quad sets: Tighten your thigh muscle and hold for 5 seconds, 10 repetitions
  • Glute squeezes: Squeeze your buttock muscles and hold 5 seconds, 10 repetitions
  • Heel slides: Slide your heel toward your buttock, keeping your foot on the bed, 10 repetitions
  • Standing march: Using a walker, lift your operated leg slightly, hold 2 seconds, 5 repetitions per side

Milestone Before Discharge

Before you leave the hospital, you should be able to get in and out of bed independently, walk short distances with a walker, go up and down stairs with supervision, and understand your hip precautions. If you cannot meet these milestones, your doctor may recommend a short stay at a rehabilitation facility.

Phase 2: Early Home Rehabilitation (Weeks 1 to 4)

Once home in Milton or the surrounding Halton Region, your focus shifts to regaining independence and building basic strength. This is when outpatient physiotherapy at Tonic Physio becomes critical for monitoring your progress and advancing your exercises safely.

Week 1 to 2: Getting Mobile at Home

Continue using your walker or crutches for all walking. Practice your hospital exercises 3 times per day. Add standing hip exercises: hip abduction (lifting your leg to the side), hip extension (lifting your leg behind you), and gentle hip flexion. Walk short distances around your home every 2 hours to prevent stiffness and improve circulation.

Week 3 to 4: Building Strength

Transition from a walker to a single crutch or cane if your surgeon approves. Start seated exercises: seated knee raises, seated hip abduction, and resistance band exercises for the outer hip muscles. Walk longer distances outdoors on flat surfaces. Your physiotherapist will assess your gait pattern and correct any limp before it becomes habitual.

Hip Precautions to Follow

Precaution Duration Why
Do not bend hip past 90 degrees 6 to 8 weeks (posterior) Prevents dislocation of the new joint
Do not cross your legs or ankles 6 to 8 weeks Maintains proper hip alignment
Do not rotate your toes inward 6 to 8 weeks Prevents posterior dislocation
Sleep with a pillow between legs 6 weeks Prevents crossing during sleep
Use a raised toilet seat 6 to 8 weeks Avoids excessive hip bending

Phase 3: Strengthening and Mobility (Weeks 5 to 12)

This phase focuses on rebuilding the muscle strength lost before and after surgery. The hip abductors (outer hip muscles) are particularly important because they stabilize your pelvis when you walk and prevent the limp that many hip replacement patients develop.

Key Exercises for Phase 3

  • Side-lying hip abduction: Lie on your unoperated side, lift your operated leg toward the ceiling, 3 sets of 12
  • Standing hip abduction with resistance band: 3 sets of 10 per side
  • Mini squats: Stand at a counter, bend knees slightly, 3 sets of 10
  • Step-ups: Step up onto a 4-inch platform, leading with the operated leg, 3 sets of 8
  • Stationary bike: Start with 5 minutes, progress to 15 minutes, no resistance initially
  • Bridging: Lie on your back, lift your hips off the floor, 3 sets of 12

Walking Progression

By week 6, most patients walk without a cane on flat surfaces. By week 8, you should be walking 20 to 30 minutes continuously. Your physiotherapy team in Milton will monitor your gait and ensure you are not developing a Trendelenburg sign, where your pelvis drops on one side due to weak abductor muscles.

Scar Tissue and Range of Motion

Surgical scar tissue can limit hip mobility if not addressed early. Your physiotherapist uses manual therapy techniques to mobilize the scar and surrounding tissue. Gentle stretching targets the hip flexors and piriformis, which often tighten after surgery. Learn more about our manual osteopathy in Milton for hands-on tissue mobilization.

Phase 4: Return to Activity (Months 3 to 12)

By month 3, most patients have returned to daily activities and light exercise. The final phase focuses on returning to the activities you love, whether that means golf, swimming, gardening, or walking the trails around Milton and the Niagara Escarpment.

Activities You Can Return To

Activity Timeline Notes
Walking (unlimited) 6 to 8 weeks Best exercise for hip replacement recovery
Swimming 6 to 8 weeks Once incision is fully healed
Stationary bike 4 to 6 weeks Start with no resistance
Golf 3 to 6 months Use a cart initially, start with chipping
Doubles tennis 6 months Avoid singles (too much pivoting)
Gardening 2 to 3 months Use raised beds, avoid deep squatting
Hiking 3 months Start with flat trails, progress gradually

Activities to Avoid Long-Term

  • High-impact sports like running, basketball, or soccer
  • Deep squatting past 90 degrees
  • Contact sports
  • Trampolining
  • Singles tennis (too much pivoting stress)

Managing Pain During Recovery

Some pain and swelling are normal during rehabilitation, but persistent or worsening pain is not. Understanding the difference helps you know when to push through and when to seek help.

Normal Pain vs Problem Pain

Mild muscle soreness after exercise that improves with rest is normal and expected. Sharp pain during weight bearing, sudden swelling, or a popping sensation could indicate dislocation or infection and requires immediate medical attention. If you experience increasing pain despite following your exercise program, our team can assess your joint pain and stiffness in Milton to determine the cause.

Ice and Elevation

Apply ice to your hip for 15 to 20 minutes after each exercise session. Elevate your leg above heart level when resting. This combination reduces swelling and speeds up tissue recovery during the first 6 weeks.

How Physiotherapy at Tonic Physio Helps

Our physiotherapy team in Milton has extensive experience with post-surgical post-surgery rehabilitation. We create individualized programs based on your surgical approach, your fitness level before surgery, and your goals for returning to activity.

Your First Appointment

At your first visit, we assess your incision healing, range of motion, muscle strength, gait pattern, and ability to perform daily activities. We review your surgeon's precautions and design a custom exercise program. Learn more about what to expect at your first physiotherapy appointment.

Ongoing Treatment Sessions

Weekly sessions include manual therapy to improve joint mobility, progressive exercise instruction, gait retraining, and functional activity practice. We adjust your program every 2 to 3 weeks based on your progress. Most patients attend physiotherapy once or twice per week for 8 to 12 weeks after hip replacement.

WSIB and Insurance Coverage

If your hip condition resulted from a workplace injury, you may qualify for WSIB coverage for your physiotherapy. Most extended health insurance plans in Ontario also cover physiotherapy after surgery. Contact our team to verify your coverage before starting treatment. We also offer WSIB care programs in Milton for workplace injury claims.

Common Complications and Warning Signs

Most hip replacements heal without major complications, but knowing the warning signs helps you catch problems early. The following complications affect a small percentage of patients and require prompt medical attention.

Blood Clots (DVT)

Deep vein thrombosis is a risk in the first 4 weeks after surgery. Symptoms include swelling in the calf, warmth, redness, and pain when pressing the area. Prevent blood clots by doing ankle pumps hourly, walking regularly, and taking any blood thinners your doctor prescribes.

Dislocation

The new hip joint is most vulnerable to dislocation in the first 6 to 8 weeks while your tissues heal. Dislocation typically occurs when you bend past 90 degrees, cross your legs, or twist your hip. If you feel a sudden pop, severe pain, or cannot bear weight, go to the emergency room immediately.

Infection

Surgical site infections affect roughly 1 to 2 percent of hip replacement patients. Watch for increasing redness, drainage, fever, or worsening pain after the first week. Early treatment with antibiotics prevents the infection from reaching the joint, which would require additional surgery.

Heterotopic Ossification

In some patients, extra bone grows in the soft tissues around the new hip joint, limiting movement. This condition, called heterotopic ossification, typically appears between 2 and 8 weeks post-surgery. Your physiotherapist monitors your range of motion and alerts your surgeon if progress stalls unexpectedly.

Frequently Asked Questions About Hip Replacement Recovery

How Long Will I Need a Walker or Cane?

Most patients use a walker for 2 to 3 weeks, then transition to a cane for 1 to 2 weeks. By week 4 to 6, many patients walk without any assistive device on flat surfaces. Your physiotherapist determines when it is safe to stop using walking aids based on your gait and balance.

When Can I Drive After Hip Replacement?

For right hip replacements, most surgeons clear driving at 4 to 6 weeks once you can brake safely without pain. For left hip replacements, you may drive as early as 2 to 3 weeks if you are off pain medications and can operate the pedals comfortably.

How Long Does the New Hip Last?

Modern hip replacements last 15 to 25 years in most patients. Longevity depends on your activity level, body weight, and how well you maintain the joint through exercise and regular movement. Low-impact activities extend the life of your replacement.

Can I Sleep on My Operated Side?

You can sleep on your operated side after 6 weeks if it is comfortable and your surgeon approves. Before that, sleep on your back or your unoperated side with a pillow between your legs to prevent crossing.

Will My Leg Lengths Be Equal After Surgery?

Your surgeon works to match leg lengths during the procedure, but slight differences can occur. Most patients adjust within 3 to 6 months. If you notice a significant difference, discuss it with your surgeon or physiotherapist. A shoe lift may be recommended temporarily.

Returning to Life in Milton After Hip Replacement

Most hip replacement patients in Milton return to driving by week 4 to 6 (once off pain medications and able to brake safely), return to work at 6 to 8 weeks for desk jobs or 10 to 12 weeks for physical jobs, and resume most recreational activities by 3 months. Your individual timeline depends on your surgical approach, your fitness before surgery, and your commitment to physiotherapy. Call us at (905) 878-7775 to book your post-surgical physiotherapy assessment, or book online through JaneApp. Our team in Milton will guide you from your first steps after surgery to a full return to the activities you love.
